title: Cancellation and timeouts
summary: Stop work that nobody is waiting for any more, and put a time limit on work that takes too long.

steps.title: Asking work to stop
body: A user closes the page while a report is loading. A search is replaced by a newer search. A call takes longer than you are willing to wait. In each case the work should **stop**, not run to the end for nobody.
C# splits cancellation over two objects:
var cts = new CancellationTokenSource();   // the remote control: you keep this
CancellationToken token = cts.Token;       // the receiver: you hand this to the work
- The **`CancellationTokenSource`** is held by whoever decides to cancel.
- The **`CancellationToken`** is passed to the code doing the work. It can only *look* at the signal, not send it.
Cancellation is **cooperative**. `Cancel()` does not kill anything. It raises a flag, and the work stops when it next checks that flag. Code that never looks at its token cannot be cancelled.

steps.prompt: Match each piece to its job.
pairs: the object that sends the cancel signal
what the working code receives and checks
`true` once the signal was sent; throws nothing
throw if the signal was sent, otherwise do nothing

steps.title: Passing the token down
body: An async method that can be cancelled takes a `CancellationToken` as its **last parameter** and passes it to every async call it makes.
static async Task<int> ImportAsync(List<string> rows, CancellationToken ct)
await SaveRowAsync(row, ct);   // pass it on
Nearly every async method in .NET accepts a token: `Task.Delay(ms, ct)`, `ReadAllTextAsync(path, ct)`, `SaveChangesAsync(ct)`, `GetAsync(url, ct)`.

When the token is cancelled, the call that is waiting throws an **`OperationCanceledException`**. It travels up through every `await`, like any exception, until someone catches it. (You may see `TaskCanceledException`: it is a subclass, so catching `OperationCanceledException` covers both.)
In a long loop that does no awaiting, check by hand with `ct.ThrowIfCancellationRequested();`.
The rule: **accept a token, pass it down**. If one method in the chain drops it, nothing below that point can be cancelled.

steps.prompt: Complete the method so it can be cancelled both during the delay and right after it.
steps.explain: Working code receives the **token**, never the source. It hands the token on to `Task.Delay`, and checks it by hand with `ThrowIfCancellationRequested()`.
The token is already cancelled, so `Task.Delay` does not wait a second. It throws at once, the `finished` line is skipped, and the `catch` runs.

steps.title: The import that would not stop
prompt: The tests provide a fake database:
public static Task SaveAsync(string row, CancellationToken ct);
`ImportAsync` saves every row and returns how many it saved. It accepts a token, and then ignores it: pressing Cancel does nothing and every row is still saved.
Fix it so that when the token is cancelled, the import stops with an `OperationCanceledException` and no further rows are saved.
starter: static async Task<int> ImportAsync(List<string> rows, CancellationToken ct)
solution: static async Task<int> ImportAsync(List<string> rows, CancellationToken ct)
template: Dojo.Eq("without a cancel, ImportAsync returns 4", 4, await ImportAsync(rows, never.Token));
Dojo.Eq("and all 4 rows were saved", 4, Store.Saved.Count);
Dojo.Eq("cancelling after row b makes ImportAsync throw OperationCanceledException", "cancelled", outcome);
Dojo.Eq("only rows a and b were saved", new List<string> { "a", "b" }, Store.Saved);
public static readonly List<string> Saved = new();
public static async Task SaveAsync(string row, CancellationToken ct)
hints: Look at what is passed to `Store.SaveAsync`. `CancellationToken.None` is a token that can never be cancelled.
The method already receives the right token as its parameter `ct`.
Change the call to `await Store.SaveAsync(row, ct);`. You do not need a `try`/`catch`: the exception should travel up to the caller.

steps.title: Timeouts are cancellation on a timer
body: A timeout is just a cancel that is sent automatically.
cts.CancelAfter(2000);                       // cancel by itself after 2 seconds
You can also give the delay to the constructor: `new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2))`.
A `CancellationTokenSource` holds a timer, so create it with `using` to clean it up when you are done.
Because this goes through the token, the work **really stops** when the time is up, as long as it passes the token down.

steps.prompt: `cts.CancelAfter(100)` fires while `CrunchAsync(cts.Token)` is running. `CrunchAsync` never looks at its token and never passes it on. What happens?
options: Nothing: `CrunchAsync` runs to the end, because cancellation is cooperative
`CrunchAsync` is stopped immediately by the runtime
An `OperationCanceledException` is thrown inside `CrunchAsync` at its next line
steps.explain: Cancelling only raises a flag on the token. Code is stopped by *its own* checks: a `ThrowIfCancellationRequested()`, or an async call that was given the token. No checks, no cancellation.

steps.title: WaitAsync: a limit on your waiting
body: Sometimes you are handed a task that takes no token, or you call code you cannot change. You can still limit how long **you** wait for it:
`task.WaitAsync(timeout)` gives a new task that finishes when the original does, or fails with a **`TimeoutException`** when the time runs out first.
Prefer a token when the work accepts one. Use `WaitAsync` when it does not.

steps.prompt: Which exception, if any, comes out of each line? (`cts.Cancel()` has already been called where it says *cancelled*.)
steps.explain: Tokens produce `OperationCanceledException`. `WaitAsync` produces `TimeoutException`. Reading `IsCancellationRequested` only gives you a `bool`, and a task that finishes in time is not affected by `WaitAsync` at all.

The work needs 5 seconds and the wait is limited to 20 ms. `WaitAsync` reports that with a `TimeoutException`. No token was involved, so nothing was cancelled, and `SlowAsync` is in fact still running.

steps.title: Fresh data or the fallback
prompt: A dashboard shows fresh data when the server answers quickly, and a cached value when it does not.
Func<CancellationToken, Task<string>> work, int timeoutMs, string fallback)
- Create a `CancellationTokenSource` that cancels itself after `timeoutMs` milliseconds.
- Call `work` with its token and await the result.
- If the work finishes in time, return its result.
- If it is cancelled by the timeout, return `fallback`.
- Any other exception from `work` is not yours to handle: let it through.
The work must really be **cancelled** through the token, not just abandoned.
starter: Func<CancellationToken, Task<string>> work, int timeoutMs, string fallback)
// create the source, set the timer, call work(token) inside a try
solution: Func<CancellationToken, Task<string>> work, int timeoutMs, string fallback)
template: string fast = await GetOrFallbackAsync(async ct => { await Task.Delay(5, ct); return "fresh"; }, 3000, "cached");
Dojo.Eq("work that finishes in time returns its own result", "fresh", fast);
Dojo.Eq("work that is too slow gives the fallback", "cached", slow);
Dojo.Check("the slow work was cancelled through its token", sawCancel, "the work ran to the end: its token was never cancelled");
try { await GetOrFallbackAsync(async ct => { await Task.Delay(5, ct); throw new InvalidOperationException("db down"); }, 3000, "cached"); }
Dojo.Eq("other exceptions are not swallowed", "InvalidOperationException", outcome);
hints: `using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource();` then `cts.CancelAfter(timeoutMs);`. Pass `cts.Token` to `work`.
Put `return await work(cts.Token);` inside a `try` block.
Add `catch (OperationCanceledException) { return fallback; }`. Catch only that type, so other exceptions still reach the caller.
